Agents that build their own databases are forcing a data foundation rethink
by Jonathan Anthony
AI agents are changing how enterprises create, move and govern information, and data observability is turning into a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have. Models get most of the attention, but the data beneath them decides whether they hold up in production.
That pressure is now reaching the cloud-native community, where KubeCon organizers added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track this year. The industry has raced from chatbots to retrieval, fine-tuning and agents, yet every wave rests on the same groundwork, according to Sanjeev Mohan (pictured), principal at SanjMo, a data and AI advisory firm, and author of "Designing the AI-Driven Data Foundations."
"AI can only be successful if it's built on a solid foundation," Mohan said. "You have no observability or transparency into it. No matter what you do on top of it, it will not be successful."
Mohan spoke with theCUBE Research's John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed theCUBE's second day of coverage at the event. (* Disclosure below.)
Why AI agents demand data observability at runtime
For decades, data was created once in an operational system and then pushed through brittle pipelines for extraction, transformation, cataloging and preparation. That model works when humans consume batch reports, Mohan explained. Thousands of agents change the math.
"They're not going to wait for this pipeline to finish. They want access to the database directly," Mohan said.
Agents are also doing something no earlier software did. They spin up short-lived databases, copy data and test different chains of thought before picking one action, according to Mohan. An agent reviewing a loan application might query census records and social media before rejecting it, which raises the question of how that decision gets audited.
"Governance becomes really important, and this is not like governance in the past where you would govern your data and then have a deterministic CFO report dashboard run on it," Mohan said.
That makes data observability part of the architecture itself, not an afterthought bolted onto a warehouse. Mohan's book, published in June 2026 by John Wiley & Sons Inc., examines how AI agents as first-class data consumers are redefining architectural principles that have stood for decades. Future platforms will need to blend structured and unstructured data in a single converged system, he noted.
"You have to save the state and you have to build the context, and this context is being built in runtime," Mohan said. "The context for the same task could be very different for the three of us. So we'll see new kinds of databases."

AI Gateway
Top AI Gateways to Reduce LLM Cost and Latency
AI gateways reduce LLM cost and latency by caching repeated prompts, routing simple requests to cheaper models, and enforcing budgets before any provider call. This guide compares Bifrost with Cloudflare AI Gateway, LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway, and Vercel AI Gateway on caching, routing, and budgets.
TL;DR
An AI gateway reduces LLM cost and latency by centralizing caching, routing, failover, budgets, and observability in one control plane, so no application team rebuilds them.
Bifrost, the open-source AI gateway built in Go, leads on both: 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 RPS, dual-layer semantic caching, a four-tier budget hierarchy, and 10,000+ models across 25+ providers under Apache 2.0.
Cloudflare caches exact-match responses only and Vercel caches none, relying on provider prompt caching; Bifrost runs exact and semantic response caching.
Cloudflare fits edge and managed stacks, LiteLLM offers Python-native provider breadth, Kong suits existing Kong estates, and Vercel fits teams built on the AI SDK.
For high-throughput or regulated teams, microsecond overhead, in-VPC deployment, and hierarchical budgets are the decisive differences, not raw provider counts.
AI gateways sit between applications and LLM providers, centralizing caching, routing, failover, governance, and observability in a single infrastructure layer. Bifrost , the open-source AI gateway by Maxim AI, leads this category with 11 microseconds of overhead per request, caching in two modes, and budget controls. Bifrost is the best choice for enterprises running mission-critical AI workloads that require top-tier performance, scalability, and reliability.
Enterprise spending on generative AI more than tripled across 2025, with foundation model API spend reaching $12.5 billion according to Menlo Ventures' State of Generative AI report. For teams running AI in production, every unoptimized API call compounds into wasted budget and degraded user experience.
The full documentation covers setup, which starts with a single npx -y @maximhq/bifrost command.
This guide breaks down the top five AI gateways to reduce LLM cost and latency and where each fits in a production stack; the 2026 ranking of the best LLM gateways covers the wider field.
Why AI Gateways Matter for LLM Cost and Latency
AI gateways reduce LLM cost and latency by centralizing all model traffic through a single control plane. Without one, every application team rebuilds the same caching, retry, and provider-management logic, and finance leaders cannot answer which team or feature is driving the bill.
The economic case has sharpened in 2026. Token unit prices have fallen sharply over two years, yet agentic models consume 5 to 30 times more tokens per task than standard chatbots , and RAG architectures inflate context windows further. Usage growth is outpacing price reduction, and unit savings only materialize for teams that own the infrastructure layer.
The optimization levers a gateway provides are:
Caching : Returns stored responses for repeated or semantically similar queries, eliminating redundant provider calls
**Failover and ** load balancing : Routes requests to alternate or cheaper models when a primary provider rate-limits or slows
Budget controls : Enforces spending limits per key, team, customer, and provider before costs accumulate
Observability : Surfaces per-model and per-team cost and latency data for informed routing decisions
Governance : Replaces shared provider keys with scoped virtual keys carrying budgets, rate limits, and model allowlists
Where LLM Cost and Latency Actually Come From
Before comparing gateways, it helps to separate the levers, because they do not all pull in the same direction. Caching and cheaper models cut spend, while every added check costs milliseconds, and the biggest latency win in agent workloads comes from making fewer model calls rather than faster ones.

Key Criteria for Evaluating AI Gateways
The best AI gateways for cost and latency remove provider calls with caching, route the remaining traffic to the cheapest capable model, stop spend at a hard limit, and add almost nothing per request. Rankings of the top LLM gateways often lead with provider count instead.
Figure 1: Response caches skip the provider call entirely; prompt caching still pays for the call, only less for the repeated prefix.
The criteria that matter most for cost and latency reduction:
Gateway overhead : The latency a gateway adds to every request. Python-based gateways often add hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds under load; compiled Go gateways add microseconds. The comparison of gateways for scaling LLMs covers behavior under sustained throughput.
Caching strategy : Exact-match caching helps, but semantic caching, which matches by meaning rather than exact text, also catches paraphrased queries at the cost of an embedding call per lookup (Figure 1).
Provider coverage : More supported providers means more flexibility for cost-optimized routing across OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Google Vertex AI, and open-source endpoints.
Budget granularity : Spending limits set at multiple levels (per key, team, customer, provider) prevent cost overruns before they happen. The LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide outlines what to look for in detail.
Observability depth : Native Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, and per-virtual-key telemetry are required for accurate cost attribution in production.
Deployment model : Self-hosted gateways give full control over data residency and air-gapped operation; managed gateways reduce operational overhead at the cost of compliance flexibility.
MCP support : Native Model Context Protocol handling , including tool filtering and token-optimization modes, decides whether agent traffic can be governed and how many tool-definition tokens each call carries.

Top 5 AI Gateways to Reduce LLM Cost and Latency
The five AI gateways below take different routes to lower LLM cost and latency: Bifrost is a self-hosted Go gateway with response caching and nested budgets, Cloudflare and Vercel are managed services, LiteLLM is a Python SDK and proxy, and Kong adds AI plugins to an API gateway.
1. Bifrost
Bifrost is a high-performance, open-source AI gateway built in Go under Apache 2.0. It unifies 10,000+ models across 25+ providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, Mistral, Groq, Cohere, Ollama, and more) through a single OpenAI-compatible API.
In sustained benchmarks at 5,000 requests per second , Bifrost adds 11 microseconds of overhead per request with a 100% success rate. In a head-to-head test against LiteLLM at 500 concurrent users, it delivered 9.5x higher throughput, 54x lower P99 latency, and 68% lower memory use.
Key cost and latency features:
Dual-layer semantic caching : The Bifrost semantic cache combines exact hash matching for byte-identical prompts with vector similarity search for semantically equivalent ones. Four vector stores are supported (Weaviate, Redis/Valkey, Qdrant, Pinecone), TTL can be overridden and the similarity threshold tightened per request, and streamed responses are cached and replayed.
Automatic prompt caching : Auto prompt caching adds cache breakpoints for clients that send none, such as Codex, so repeated prefixes bill at the provider's cache-read rate.
Four-tier budget hierarchy : Hierarchical budgets enforce spending limits at the customer, team, virtual key, and provider-config levels simultaneously, with independent reset schedules. Requests exceeding any active cap are rejected inline with HTTP 402 before a token reaches a provider.
Automatic failover, weighted routing, and adaptive load balancing : Fallback chains route requests to alternate providers after retries when a provider becomes unavailable, weighted distribution lets teams split traffic across providers (for example, 80/20 between a cost-effective and premium option), and Enterprise adaptive routing shifts traffic by live error rates and latency.
Native MCP gateway : Bifrost acts as both MCP client and server. Code Mode lets the model write Python (Starlark) to orchestrate multiple tools in a single execution, cutting input tokens by up to 92.8% and running about 40% faster in large MCP deployments. Tool filtering can be applied per virtual key.
Built-in observability : Native Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry integration surface token usage, latency, cache hit rates, and per-virtual-key cost data in real time, with Grafana, New Relic, Honeycomb, and Datadog compatibility.
Enterprise security and compliance : RBAC with SSO through Okta and Entra, in-VPC deployment , vault and cloud key management integrations, and HMAC-signed audit logs of administrative activity suitable for SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, and ISO 27001 reviewers.
Drop-in SDK replacement : Bifrost is a drop-in replacement for the OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, LiteLLM, LangChain, and PydanticAI SDKs. Teams change only the base URL; no application rewrites are required.
Best for: Bifrost is built for enterprises running mission-critical AI workloads that require top-tier performance, scalability, and reliability. It serves as a centralized AI gateway to route, govern, and secure all AI traffic across models and environments with ultra low latency. Bifrost unifies LLM gateway , MCP gateway, and Agents gateway capabilities into a single platform. Designed for regulated industries and strict enterprise requirements, it supports air-gapped deployments, VPC isolation, and on-prem infrastructure. It provides full control over data, access, and execution, along with strong security, policy enforcement, and governance capabilities.
2. Cloudflare AI Gateway
Cloudflare AI Gateway is a managed service that runs on Cloudflare's edge network. Analytics, caching, and rate limiting are free on all plans, with no infrastructure to manage.
Key cost and latency features:
Edge caching : Identical requests are served from Cloudflare's cache for up to one month
Rate limiting : Protects against quota exhaustion and prevents runaway API costs from unexpected traffic spikes
Spend limits : Cost-based budgets by model, provider, or custom metadata such as user or team
Auto Router : cloudflare/auto weighs expected quality against cost to pick a model per request
Logging and Workers integration : Logs with token and cost data, OpenTelemetry export, and tight coupling with Workers AI
Caching applies only to identical requests, so paraphrased prompts still reach the provider. Spend limits are eventually consistent and do not nest into a customer, team, and key hierarchy, and self-hosted deployment is not available.
Best for: teams on Cloudflare that need managed caching, rate limiting, spend limits, and centralized logging without dedicated AI infrastructure.
3. LiteLLM
LiteLLM is an open-source Python SDK and proxy server that provides a unified OpenAI-compatible interface to over 100 LLM providers. Since v1.110.0, its routing logic runs in a Rust core while authentication, configuration, and callbacks stay in Python; the LiteLLM Rust gateway buyer checklist covers what changes.
Key cost and latency features:
Broad provider coverage : Supports 100+ providers including niche and open-weight model hosting platforms
Budgets and spend tracking : Key, user, team, and customer budgets, backed by Postgres
Routing and retries : Cost-, latency-, and usage-based routing with fallbacks and retries across providers
Caching : Exact and semantic caching on Redis/Valkey or Qdrant, plus S3 and in-memory caches
Python-native integration : Direct integration into Python codebases through callbacks and hooks
The Python runtime adds measurably more latency overhead per request than compiled alternatives: LiteLLM's own benchmark reports 8 ms of p95 overhead at 1,170 RPS, where Bifrost adds 11 microseconds. The March 2026 PyPI supply chain incident also raised concerns for enterprise deployments that rely on Python package distribution. Teams evaluating a migration can review Bifrost as a LiteLLM alternative for a feature-by-feature comparison.
Best for: Python-first teams running low-to-moderate traffic that need a unified API across many providers and value SDK-level integration.
4. Kong AI Gateway
Kong AI Gateway extends Kong's API management platform to support LLM routing. For organizations already managing traditional API traffic through Kong, it consolidates API and AI infrastructure under one control plane.
Key cost and latency features:
Unified API and AI governance : Manage traditional APIs and LLM traffic with the same policies, rate limits, and authentication
Token analytics and cost limits : Usage analytics for tokens, errors, and latency, plus token and cost limits per consumer group
Semantic caching and prompt compression : AI Semantic Cache and AI Prompt Compressor plugins
Plugin ecosystem : mTLS, role-based access control, and request transformation through Kong's existing plugins
Kong AI Gateway is most effective when Kong is already in the stack. Teams adopting it solely for LLM routing face a steeper learning curve and a heavier infrastructure footprint. Semantic caching, advanced AI rate limiting, and the AI MCP Proxy for MCP gateway traffic require an AI Gateway Enterprise license, and nested multi-level budgets are not documented.
Best for: enterprises standardized on Kong for traditional API management that want to extend the same control plane to LLM traffic.
5. Vercel AI Gateway
Vercel AI Gateway is a hosted API that works natively with the Vercel AI SDK and accepts OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible requests from any cloud; applications do not need to run on Vercel.
Key cost and latency features:
Native SDK integration : Works by default with the Vercel AI SDK, reducing setup time
No token markup : Provider list prices with no platform fee, including bring-your-own-key requests
Prompt caching : caching: 'auto' adds provider cache markers so repeated prefixes bill at the cache-read rate
Budgets and cost-sorted routing : Team, project, key, and user budgets return HTTP 402 once exceeded, and providers can be sorted by cost or latency
Built-in analytics : Request logs and OpenTelemetry trace drains
Vercel AI Gateway does not cache responses, budgets do not cover bring-your-own-key traffic, and self-hosted deployment is not available.
Best for: teams building on the Vercel AI SDK that want a hosted, zero-markup API with provider failover and budgets.
How AI Gateways Route Requests to Cheaper Models
Routing to a cheaper model saves money only when that model can still answer the request; otherwise retries erase the savings. All five gateways now offer some form of cost-aware routing, from per-request model selection to sorting a model's providers by price.
Figure 2: Cheap-model routing is a rule on a tier or a budget percentage, so application code keeps calling one model name.
In Bifrost, routing rules are CEL expressions where the first match wins. The Complexity Router tags each request Simple, Medium, or Complex, so complexity_tier == "SIMPLE" can go to a low-cost model, while budget_used > 80 moves traffic to a fallback as a budget fills. Classification runs only when a rule references the tier; a decision-model call typically takes 600-800 ms, and the semantic classifier is usually much faster.
The guide to how model routing works compares routing strategies, and the Bifrost vs LiteLLM router comparison tests two of them side by side.
How to Choose the Right AI Gateway
Choose an AI gateway by where cost and latency accrue and where the team already runs. High-volume, multi-team, or regulated workloads need response caching, nested budgets, and self-hosting; teams committed to Cloudflare, Vercel, or Kong can start with that platform's gateway.
Figure 3: Platform commitments decide most choices; self-hosting, semantic caching, and nested budgets point to Bifrost.
High-throughput, regulated, or multi-team enterprises : Hierarchical budgets, in-VPC deployment, MCP support, and microsecond-level overhead. The open-source Bifrost gateway is purpose-built for this profile, and the enterprise LLM deployment comparison covers the full requirement set.
Cloudflare-native applications : Cloudflare AI Gateway works for exact-match caching, rate limiting, and spend limits when compliance requirements are modest; this production-ready LLM gateway comparison adds more options.
Python-only, lower-volume workloads : LiteLLM remains viable for teams that want SDK-level integration and can absorb the Python runtime overhead.
Kong-native API platforms : Kong AI Gateway fits when the team already runs Kong for traditional APIs.
AI SDK applications : Vercel AI Gateway is the natural choice when the application is built on the Vercel AI SDK, whether or not it is hosted on Vercel.
Any gateway that cannot enforce budgets inline, attribute every call to a virtual key, and recover automatically from provider outages should not be the only thing between an application and a production LLM bill.
Reduce LLM Cost and Latency with Bifrost
AI gateways have moved from optional tooling to required infrastructure for any team running LLM workloads in production. Semantic caching, multi-provider failover, hierarchical budget enforcement, and real-time observability together translate into lower costs and faster responses.
Bifrost delivers these capabilities with 11 microseconds of overhead per request at 5,000 RPS, an Apache 2.0 license, and enterprise-grade governance, and the published performance benchmarks document the headroom in detail. To see how Bifrost can reduce LLM cost and latency in your environment, book a demo with the Bifrost team.
Frequently Asked Questions
How do AI gateways reduce LLM cost and latency?
A gateway centralizes caching, routing, failover, budgets, and observability, so optimizations apply once across every application. Semantic caching removes redundant provider calls, weighted routing shifts traffic to cheaper or faster providers, inline budgets stop overruns before a token is spent, and per-request telemetry shows where cost and latency accumulate.
Does an AI gateway add latency?
A well-engineered gateway adds negligible latency. Bifrost adds roughly 11 microseconds of overhead per request at 5,000 RPS, orders of magnitude smaller than provider response times. Cache lookups add their own time, since a semantic lookup needs an embedding call, but the failover and caching a gateway provides usually reduce end-to-end latency far more than the gateway hop adds.
What is the difference between exact-match and semantic caching?
Exact-match caching returns a stored response only when a prompt is character-for-character identical, so hit rates are low in natural language. Semantic caching matches by meaning using embeddings and a similarity threshold, so paraphrased prompts hit the cache and skip the provider call. Bifrost's semantic caching runs the exact hash first and falls back to the embedding search only on a miss, so identical prompts never pay for an embedding.
Can budget controls prevent cost overruns in real time?
Yes, if they enforce inline rather than report after the fact. Bifrost's four-tier budgets sit at the customer, team, virtual key, and provider level, and a request exceeding any active cap is rejected with an HTTP 402 before it reaches a provider. This stops a runaway agent loop before it becomes a bill, rather than flagging it on next month's invoice. The pattern for per-user budgets and automatic fallbacks shows a full setup.
Which AI gateway is best for reducing LLM cost and latency?
For high-throughput or regulated production workloads, Bifrost is the best AI gateway for cost and latency: 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 RPS, dual-layer semantic caching, four-tier budgets, and self-hosting under Apache 2.0. Cloudflare fits edge stacks, LiteLLM suits Python-first breadth, Kong fits existing Kong estates, and Vercel fits AI SDK applications. The best LLM gateways guide ranks the wider field.

Akamai to Acquire API Protection Startup Noname Security for $450 Million
Akamai has announced plans to acquire Noname Security to enhance its API protection offering.
Ionut Arghire
| May 7, 2024 (9:53 AM ET)
Flipboard
Reddit
Whatsapp
Email
Cloud and security giant Akamai on Tuesday announced plans to acquire application programming interface (API) protection company Noname Security.
Founded in 2020, the San Jose, California-based Noname is one of the top API security vendors, reaching unicorn status in 2021 , one year after emerging from stealth. The company has raised $220 million in funding.
Noname will help Akamai expand its existing API Security solution to meet customer demand and market requirements. The acquisition will also allow Akamai to scale its sales and marketing resources.
Akamai says the acquisition will allow it to provide a complete API security suite covering shadow APIs, as well as vulnerability and attack detection.
Additionally, Akamai's Application and API platform customers will benefit from Noname's integration shortly after the acquisition is completed.
As part of the deal, which is expected to close in the second quarter of 2024, Akamai will pay out roughly $450 million for all the outstanding equity of Noname. The cloud giant expects the transaction to deliver roughly $20 million in revenue for the fiscal year 2024.

Noname has more than 200 employees, all of whom, including the CEO and co-founder Oz Golan, are expected to join Akamai following the deal's completion.
"Combining Noname with Akamai's API Security offering will provide a solution for any type of customer. No matter where the customer's applications reside - be it in the cloud, natively on the edge, on-premise, or on other vendor platforms - they will be protected," Golan said.

Red Hat accelerates agentic adoption across hybrid environments
by Devony Hof
Enterprise ambitions for artificial intelligence are outpacing the infrastructure and budgets needed to support them. Red Hat AI faces a familiar enterprise challenge: turning ambitious plans for artificial intelligence into production deployments that deliver measurable returns.
Organizations must also decide how to deploy and manage increasingly complex AI workloads across existing infrastructure without letting costs spiral. At Red Hat Summit 2026 in May, Red Hat Inc. outlined its approach to those challenges through expanded platform capabilities, automation and an open-source development process that relies on community contributions.
"I think everybody here loves that because that does lead to sovereignty as well," said Rob Strechay , principal analyst at theCUBE, during the event . "They're actually building on top of open source and enhancing it in a way that provides more value in supporting it, which is key to their success."
This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media's ongoing coverage of the AWS Financial Services Symposium. (* Disclosure below.)
Red Hat expands support for AI across hybrid cloud environments
Deploying and managing AI workloads across hybrid cloud environments presents new operational challenges for enterprises. Red Hat's answer is Red Hat AI 3.4, an updated version of its enterprise AI platform that supports agentic AI deployments and large-scale inference across hybrid environments.
The company also announced two new managed services : Red Hat AI Inference and Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization Service on IBM Cloud. Red Hat AI Inference is designed to integrate real-time AI inference directly into clients' production workflows, while OpenShift Virtualization enables clients to migrate and run virtual machines at scale. Both services are intended to accelerate hybrid cloud adoption .
"What's really going to drive inference demand exponentially is AI agents," said Joe Fernandes , vice president and general manager of Red Hat AI. "We provide a platform where customers can deploy and manage their AI agents across a hybrid infrastructure environment."
The next piece of Red Hat's agentic strategy comes in the form of Ansible Automation Platform 2.7 , which connects AI-generated insights to governed infrastructure actions. Its self-service automation capabilities allow authorized users in locations such as branch offices and factory floors to manage servers and networks within established controls.
"Customers are now able to use their own data to calculate savings and efficiencies ," said Sathish Balakrishnan , vice president and general manager of Red Hat's Ansible business unit. "Every action, whether it's triggered by humans, an event or an AI agent, passes through the same [access controls], approval gates, audit trails, content signing and credential management."
New services aim to mitigate AI budget concerns
AI budgets are booming: according to theCUBE Research , Analysts project that AI cloud spending could approach $2.5 trillion by 2026, growing at roughly 44% year-over-year. However, that investment does not always return concrete value. Research shows that 50.7% of organizations rely on public AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot but only 20.2% report enterprise-wide AI deployments built on a governed framework.
"Most people are token consumers and that is part of the reason they're trying to figure out how do they get to production," Strechay said. "How do they get out of these death-by-pilot situations and become token producers so that they can offset the cost or at least lower the cost so they can get to the [return on AI investment] of those applications? You can use [OpenShift] infrastructure along with things like vLLM and some of the other things in Red Hat AI to get and become efficient in how you produce your tokens."
Part of Red Hat's strategy for helping customers manage sprawling AI budgets is its partnership with Advanced Micro Devices, Inc . Together, AMD and Red Hat are encouraging enterprises to rethink the financials of AI. Rather than opting for the newest, most expensive hardware, clients might have better results if matching compute resources to the workload, according to John Hampton , corporate vice president of global enterprise technical sales at AMD.
"So many of these enterprises just ran out and bought big [graphics processing unit] clusters because they knew they had to solve for AI," he said. "Enterprises are coming to us and saying, 'This is exploding. It's good that we're using AI, but we can't afford this anymore.'"
Red Hat has also joined forces with Intel Corp. to help customers determine which combination of hardware and software best suits their workloads. As enterprises look to reduce inference costs, the companies are emphasizing the value of choosing the right mix of CPUs and GPUs rather than relying on a single approach.
"As we've gone through this with our customers in the industry , we've seen that people often have just assumed, 'I've got a hammer. I need the nail to hit it with,'" said Bill Pearson , vice president of data center and AI at Intel. "Once they take a step back to say, 'Wait a minute. I have these [central processing units] in my data center' or 'I need to figure out how to balance the right number of CPUs with the right number of GPUs to achieve that outcome I'm looking for,' they're actually going to get better results at a better price point for delivering lower-cost tokens."
Red Hat AI partnerships extend from enterprise agents to the edge
Red Hat announced several collaborations at the summit, including Red Hat AI Factory with Nvidia Corp. The partnership includes support for Nvidia's Blackwell architecture and upcoming Vera Rubin platform, as well as participation in Nvidia's OpenShell project for AI agent sandboxing and secure execution.
"Moving AI from corporate experimentation to an industrial engine requires a sovereign, consistent foundation across the hybrid cloud," said Chris Wright , chief technology officer and senior vice president for global engineering at Red Hat, in the announcement . "Through our strategic co-engineering efforts with Nvidia, Red Hat provides the architectural control and open source innovation enterprises need to scale agentic AI with confidence."
Red Hat's other partnership announcements focused on agentic AI and edge computing. Boomi LP, which brands itself as a data activation company, is collaborating with Red Hat on a single, integrated stack for deploying agentic AI at scale . The partnerships with Panasonic Connect and Voyager cover edge computing solutions and space edge micro data centers, respectively.
Red Hat's expanding ecosystem of partnerships reflects the growing range of enterprise applications for agentic AI. The challenge for organizations is determining how those capabilities can address their specific business needs, according to Matt Hicks, president and chief executive officer of Red Hat.
"From the board level down ... you have a feeling of, 'We have to be able to harness what this technology can do,'" said Matt Hicks . "The people that will be the most successful with AI are the people that have the most questions. People that know business, they know their domain. Those are the ones [that] have no barriers to what they can do and change. It's just about getting started."
Red Hat expands sovereign AI capabilities and governance
Sovereign AI has become an increasingly important consideration for enterprises seeking greater control over their data and infrastructure. Gartner Inc. forecasts that the sovereign cloud infrastructure-as-a-service market will grow at a compound annual rate of 36% through 2028.
Red Hat is expanding support for sovereign cloud while allowing customers to keep the infrastructure they already invested in. That includes collaborations with Core42 , which specializes in sovereign-by-design infrastructure, and Sopra Steria , a longstanding European collaborator on sovereign AI initiatives.
Red Hat is also extending its software security capabilities as enterprises adopt agentic AI. Fedora Hummingbird Linux is a container-native operating system designed for agent-first development, with an automated software delivery pipeline . Meanwhile, Red Hat Hardened Images provides a catalog of minimal container images designed to reduce vulnerabilities and strengthen software supply-chain security.
At this point, sovereign AI and governance play an essential role in giving customers choice and control , according to Ashesh Badani , senior vice president and chief product officer of Red Hat.
"Whether an organization is meeting jurisdictional mandates or reclaiming its data from proprietary silos, we are providing the capabilities and platforms to build a more self-determined future," he said in a Red Hat press release .
